site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Wise Merchant's Careful Journey
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Two merchants set out across the long, hot sandy road, their carts heavy with goods. One, trusting strangers who promised water ahead, poured his supplies away and suffered cruelly when none appeared beneath the burning sun.

The wiser merchant looked closely and saw that the travelers' clothes and wagon wheels were dry, proof of their trickery. He kept his water safe, rested through the noon heat, and moved forward in the cool night air.

By morning his people and goods arrived safely on the far side, his patience and careful eyes rewarded by the journey's success. The sandy road became not a danger, but a quiet triumph of thoughtfulness over hardship.

stories.title: The Golden Deer King Steps Forward
stories.source: Nigrodhamiga Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a royal park, a human king kept two herds of deer and claimed one each day for his table. To end the terror of the hunt, the deer themselves chose to take turns, sending one of their own in peaceful surrender to the executioner.

Among them lived Nigrodha, the golden Deer King, wise and beloved. When a pregnant doe approached him with quiet pleading, afraid her fawn would be chosen before it was even born, Nigrodha did not hesitate. He offered himself in her place and walked gently toward the king.

Learning the reason for Nigrodha's sacrifice, the king was softened by such selfless compassion. He released the noble deer and the mother doe, then set every deer in the park free, extending his protection to all animals across his realm, and the herds lived safely beneath his care.

stories.title: Three Friends, One Brave Rescue
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: In the quiet forest, three devoted friends—a deer, a turtle, and a woodpecker—shared their days together. One morning a hunter's cruel net caught the deer among the trees, and the kind-hearted turtle hurried over to bite through the thick cords, while the clever woodpecker flew toward the hunter's path to buy them time.

The woodpecker darted near the hunter's home, calling out as if dawn had come far too soon and warning that misfortune waited outside his door. Confused and uneasy, the man lingered indoors, never guessing that his small feathered visitor was really shielding a life. The turtle worked without stopping, gnawing strand by strand.

When the hunter finally reached the snare, the deer bounded away into the green woods, and the turtle slipped gently into the water. Soon the three friends found one another again, their hearts light with joy, for courage and cooperation had turned a trap into a triumph of love.

stories.title: The Golden Dish of Seri
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: Two merchants journeyed through a town buying old household goods. A poor girl offered one of them a worn dish, and the merchant, quick with greed, tested it and found it was solid gold. He smiled to himself, lied that it was worthless, and promised to return, thinking to claim the treasure for himself later.

The second merchant came that same day and saw at once what the dish truly was. Without hesitation, he gave the girl all the money and goods he carried, a fair and open-hearted exchange that left her astonished and her grandmother beaming at such kindness.

When the dishonest merchant returned, he discovered the golden dish already gone, sold for a song by his own deception. The girl and her grandmother were safe and prosperous, while the honest merchant walked on lighter, his generosity rewarded with the blessing of a kind deed well done.

stories.title: The Bridge of the Monkey King
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: In a forest where a mango tree leaned over a river, the monkey king watched with alarm as men closed in around his troop, hungry for both fruit and capture. The animals had nowhere to run, and the humans prepared their nets.

The king leaped to a far bank and stretched his body across the rushing water, becoming a living bridge for his troop. One by one the monkeys scrambled over his aching back to safety, and at last every one of them stood free on the distant shore.

Though his limbs trembled with exhaustion, the king rejoiced to see his troop unharmed. The men, astonished by such self-giving courage, lowered their nets and let the monkeys go, honoring a leader who had loved his people more than himself.
